subject: Accountancy
central_question: How are business transactions supported by documents, analysed through the accounting equation and recorded through debit, credit, journal and ledger?
in_scope_units: Business transactions, source documents and vouchers.
Preparation and essential elements of transaction, debit, credit and journal vouchers.
Accounting equation and its application to transactions.
Rules of debit and credit for assets, liabilities, capital, expenses, losses, revenues and gains.
Journal as the book of original entry, journalising, narration and compound entries.
Ledger as the principal book, posting and balancing of accounts.
banned_topics: Special-purpose books and cash-book variants, which belong to Recording of Transactions – II.
Trial balance and rectification of errors, which belong to Chapter 6.
Preparation of final accounts, which belongs to Chapters 8 and 9.

known_pitfalls.claim: Debit always means increase and credit always means decrease.
known_pitfalls.correction: Debit increases assets and expenses but decreases liabilities, capital and revenue; credit has the opposite effects.

known_pitfalls.claim: A transaction voucher and source document are always the same physical document.
known_pitfalls.correction: A source document evidences the transaction; an accounting voucher may be prepared from that evidence for recording.

known_pitfalls.claim: The accounting equation changes only when cash changes.
known_pitfalls.correction: Every measurable transaction may affect assets, liabilities or capital even without cash movement.

known_pitfalls.claim: Journal and ledger perform the same function.
known_pitfalls.correction: The journal records transactions chronologically; the ledger classifies them account-wise.

known_pitfalls.claim: A compound entry can contain only one debit and one credit.
known_pitfalls.correction: A compound entry involves more than two accounts while total debits still equal total credits.

recommended_example_progression: Use the ₹35,000 computer cash memo example in section 3.1 to identify a transaction and source document.
Use Example 1 on Rohit to trace the accounting equation from capital ₹5,00,000 to the final equation ₹6,80,000 = ₹1,70,000 + ₹5,10,000.
Use Illustration 1 to practise ten effects on A = L + C.
Use the Rohit transactions for furniture, plant, purchases, sales, rent and salary to apply debit and credit rules.
Use the chapter journal and ledger illustrations to practise journalising, narration, posting and balancing.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter ends with Short Answer Questions, Long Answer Questions, numerical exercises on the accounting equation, journalising and ledger posting, and a Checklist to Test Your Understanding.
